original.verbatim:
Here is the HTML code for a drop-down list which consists of 3 colors: red, green, and blue.

```
<select>
  <option value="red">Red</option>
  <option value="green">Green</option>
  <option value="blue">Blue</option>
</select>
```

This code creates a select element with 3 option elements inside it. Each option element represents a color: red, green, or blue. The "value" attribute of each option element contains the value that will be submitted when the form is submitted. In this case, the values are "red", "green", and "blue".

To define text content in JavaScript, you can declare a variable and assign it a string value. Here are some examples:

``` javascript
var message = "Hello, world!"; // Defines a variable 'message' with the string value "Hello, world!"
```

``` javascript
var greeting = "Welcome to our website."; // Defines a variable 'greeting' with the string value "Welcome to our website."
```

``` javascript
var paragraph = "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit."; // Defines a variable 'paragraph' with the string value "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit."
```

Once you have defined a variable with a text content, you can use it in your code to display it on the page, or manipulate it in various ways.

For example, to display the value of a variable on a web page, you can use the innerHTML property of an HTML element:

``` javascript
var message = "Hello, world!";
var output = document.getElementById("output");
output.innerHTML = message;
```

This code first defines a variable `message` with the text content "Hello, world!", and then retrieves a reference to an HTML element with the ID "output" using the `getElementById()` method. Finally, it sets the `innerHTML` property of the element to the value of the `message` variable, which causes the text content to be displayed on the page.
